en: The Yājñavalkya-Śikṣā composed by the seer Śrī Yājñavalkya:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the characteristics of the three accents (trai-svarya):
namely, the acute (udātta), the grave (anudātta), and likewise the circumflex (svarita).
I shall describe the characteristics, the presiding deity, and the very location [of the accents].
One should know that the acute (udātta) is white; the grave (anudātta) is said to be red;
one should recognize the circumflex (svarita) as dark-blue; and Agni is the deity of the acute. 1–2.
One should know that the low tone (nīca) is Soma; the acute tone (svarita) is Savitṛ. One should recognize the acute (udātta) as Brāhmaṇa, while the low (nīca) is said to be Kṣatriya.
One should know the circumflex (svarita) as Vaiśya, and the acute (udātta) as Bhāradvāja.
They say that the *gāyatrī* is low (*nīca*), and they know the *gārgya* to be circumflex (*svarita*).
One should know the *gāyatrī* to be acute (*udātta*), while the *traiṣṭubha* is said to be low, and the *jāgata* should be known as circumflex; thus it is by rule.
Those seven notes, beginning with *ṣaḍja*, which are proclaimed in the *Gāndharvaveda*,
are to be understood as the three notes, beginning with *ucca*, in the *Veda*. Among them,
*niṣāda* and *gāndhāra* are high (*ucca*), while *ṛṣabha* and *dhaivata* are low (*nīca*).
The remaining notes—Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Pañcama—are to be known as svarita (circumflex).
In the Veda, Ṣaḍja is the peacock; Ṛṣabha is at the mouth of the goat;
they low toward Gāndhāra with their voices; and the Kauñcas [low] toward Madhyama.
Kaukila is to be known as the fifth; Gaja, however, speaks of Niṣāda;
and Āśva is to be known as Dhaivata—thus the seven notes (svaras) are prescribed. A moment (nimeṣa) is the measure of time, and others say it is the duration of a flash of lightning.
From the syllable and through its equal conjunction, there arises the cognition of Somaśarman.
Where a tiny particle (kaṇikā) is seen, resembling a ray of the sun— that is the measure (mātrā) of the atom (aṇu), and that measure consists of four atoms.
One should know that at the mind there is one atom (aṇu); at the throat, two atoms;

and at the tip of the tongue, three atoms. They know that which has issued forth [from the mouth] to be measured by a single mora (mātrika). In the case of a hiatus (avagraha), however, the duration is prescribed as half a mora.
Between the two feet, a duration of one *mātrā* is prescribed for the *kāla*.
However, at the end of a *ṛc*, it should be two *mātrās*, and at the very end of the *ṛc*, it should be three *mātrās*.
Having raised the empty hand, the wise man should maintain it for two *mātrās*.
A short vowel should be known as having one mātrā; a long vowel is said to have two mātrās; and a protracted (pluta) vowel should be understood as having three mātrās. A consonant has half a mātrā.
[This applies] in the open position (vivṛti), at the end of speech (avasāna), and likewise in other cases such as the half-mora of the vowel ṛ.
At the word and at the pause, it is prescribed that the hands be empty;
one should perform the *praṇava* as a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, while the wise know the *vyāhṛtis* to be the *mātṛkās*.
The blue jay utters a single *mātrā*, while the crow has spoken of two *mātrās*.
The crested one (Śikhin) speaks of the three measures; such is the established order of measures.
Color, caste, measure, lineage, meter, and deity—all this has been fully explained by the wise Yājñavalkya. 17–18.
The two hands should be held restrained, positioned above the knees;
one should perform what is authorized by the teacher, reciting [the text] without having any other thought.
Having placed the right hand on the third part of the thighs, [one should remain thus].
Having become serene in mind, with his face slightly lowered and turned downward,
he should first employ the *praṇava*, followed by the *vyāhṛtis*, and then the *sāvitrī* in their proper sequence; thereafter, he should commence the Vedas.
Withdrawing his movements like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, the wise man—steadfast, tranquil, and fearless—should pronounce the phonemes with firm vision and mind.
He should not strike them, nor should he suppress them; he should neither sing them out nor cause them to tremble.
Just as one should pronounce the phonemes, so too should one bring them to completion.
Fixing one's gaze upon the tips of the fingers, one should contemplate the meaning of the scripture; one should pronounce the phonemes equally with both the hand and the mouth. 23–24.
Both the tone and the hand must occur simultaneously;
one who has failed in the hand or failed in the tone does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda.
One should not be hideous, nor have protruding lips, nor be indistinct, nor nasalized.
One who is stammering or whose tongue is tied is not fit to utter the phonemes. He whose nature is auspicious, whose teeth and lips are beautiful,
and who is both confident and modest is fit to utter the phonemes.

Doubtful, frightened, excited, indistinct, nasalized, crow-like, reaching the head, and likewise devoid of its proper place; discordant, tasteless, disjointed, and struck unevenly—(these are defects of recitation). 28.
Confused, lacking the palate [proper articulation], and the fourteen defects of recitation;
abounding in the essence of the *saṃhitā*, confused by the designations of words (*pada*), and filled with the junctions of the *krama*—the ocean of mantras is difficult to cross. (29–30)
Having recited the *Ṛg-saṃhitā* three times, or the *Yajus* with a concentrated mind,
or the *Sāmans* along with their secret doctrines, one is liberated from all sins. The *Saṃhitā* leads one to the solar station and the lunar station.
The sequence leads gradually to that subtle state which is free from affliction (32). The *Kālindī-saṃhitā* should be known as being joined with the *pada*s;
one should cause the *Gaṅgā* to revolve in sequence, for the speech of Śambhu is not otherwise (33).
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does all evil conduct sink away when immersed in the threefold Veda. [Likewise,
one should use] the leaves of the mango, palāśa, and bilva, and of apāmārga and śirīṣa.
Rising in the morning with speech restrained, he should consume the tooth-cleansing stick.
The *khadira*, *kadamba*, *karavīra*, and *karañjaka*—these thorny trees are auspicious; those with milky sap are glorious. (35–36)

By its preparation, a subtle sweetness arises; the disciple should always consume it with Triphalā mixed with salt. This [preparation] generates diminished intellect, as well as [improves] the voice and complexion. 37
Those who know the Vedas understand that a mantra recited by one who lacks his hands does not accomplish the *yajus* formulas,
just as food eaten without condiments. (38) Furthermore, he who recites [a mantra] lacking his hands, devoid of proper accents and phonemes—
One who is consumed by the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas] enters a low birth.
He who recites the *Ṛks*, *Yajus*, and *Sāmans* without using his hands remains a Brahmin devoid of the *Ṛks* as long as he does not find the *Svāra* [melody]. 39–40.
Likewise, the meaning of the Vedas must be understood for the successful accomplishment of ritual acts;

for by reciting them merely through incorrect pronunciation, one sinks like a cow in the mud. (41) One who employs the correct accents and phonemes, yet practices what has been studied only with his hand [without understanding], [does not attain the fruit].
Purified by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
One should not make the step too long, nor should one make it too slow;
the seizing and releasing of the step should be like the swift movement of a horse.
One should diligently apply oneself to the scripture, for its essence is that very cause;
while reciting, one should maintain a composed countenance and not allow the mind to wander elsewhere.
One should not clench the fists, nor should one behave with excessive arrogance.
The *culurnaukā*, the *sphuṭa*, the *daṇḍī*, the *svastika*, and the shape of a *muṣṭi*—these indeed are the defects of the hand, with the *paraśu* being the seventh.
As is the speech, so are the hands; one should therefore avoid that which is empty.

Wherever the voice is situated, the hand remains right there. (46) Just as when an arrow is released from a drawn bow, the string returns to its own place, so too does the sound remain within the hand. (47)

One should form the *svaraviddha* hand, held slightly upward with the fingers somewhat clearly colored and extended toward the region of the *prādeśa*. That which occurs above the first joint of the thumb and over the index finger is [the *svaraviddha*]. 48.
One should move the hand only that much, together with its designated area, for the *prādeśa* measurement.
Having raised it to the height of the *manuṣyatīrtha*, one should proceed toward the water at the *pitṛtīrtha*;
the back of the hand is bent, while the release of the fingers is clearly visible.

One should know that in the case of a *svarita* there are three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), in a *nipāta* six finger-breadths, and in an *utthāna* nine finger-breadths; this is the characteristic of the accent (*svara*).
For the purpose of practice one should use a rapid tempo (*drutā vṛtti*), but for the purpose of performance a medium tempo (*madhyamā*).
For the purpose of instructing disciples, one should employ a slow tempo (vilambita-vṛtti). The Aindra tempo is moderate, while the Prājāpatya is slow;
however, the Agnimāruta tempo is censured in all treatises.
At the letter *ma*, the form is that of a fist; at *na*, it is from the tips of the fingernails;
at the *anusvāra*, there is the throwing of the thumb; and at the end of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), there is the release of the fingers.
(54) The *udātta* accent is indicated by a downward movement toward the ground, while the *pracaya* is neither harsh nor intense.
The remainder should be known as six *aṅgulas*, and it is prescribed that this should be well-compacted.
For a hand of noble birth and for one that follows the [standard] proportions, it is six *aṅgulas*;
one should fashion the hand using a measure of exactly one-fourth of that.
At the end of *ka* and at the end of *ṭa*, one should bend the fingers *ṅa* and *ṇa*;
at *a* and *ta*, the five fingers take the form of a coil (57).
That which arises from throwing [the hands] upward is *yoṣmā*, and that which arises from throwing them downward is [also so].
The wise man should release [the fingers] one by one during a svarita; however, during both [svarita and pluta], he should throw them both down.

The contraction of the thumb is prescribed for the attainment [of the goal]; for the anusvāra, the water-offering (arghya); and for the long vowel and the raṅga, the extension of the index finger is proclaimed. 58–59.
Even upon the contact of the index finger and the thumb, the *udātta* accent is perceived;
however, one should make the *madhyama* low, and the remainder progressively lower (*nīcatara*). Whatever becomes *svarita*, it is joined with a slight opening of the mouth (*vakāra*).
One should recognize that as the *ūṣman*; it should be placed after both [the preceding and following vowels].

When a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) is seen where a *svarita* has been placed, it should be inserted after the one with two morae (*dvimātrika*), but in the case of one with a single mora (*ekamātrika*), one should insert it after both. 1.67.61–62.
Wherever the letter *va* is seen in both the *jātya* and the *svarita* accents, the view is that an elision of both should be performed;
it is like the horns of a calf, or like the pair of breasts of a young maiden. (63)

Where there is a vowel followed by a *visarga* and a *svarita* accent, that is declared to be *ubhakṣepa*. Where a vowel ending in a *visarga* is seen to have a *svarita* accent, and where there is both a long vowel and the particle *tu*, there it is called *ubhakṣepa*. 64–65.
Heat (ūṣman) may be of three kinds: pracita, balakāntara, and svarita.
One should know that pracita occurs in svarita, while balakā is known to occur in nipāta;
likewise, tāra occurs in utthāna. By means of these three heats—
But having discerned each measure (mātrā), one should then apply the pause (kṣepa).
One [syllable] partakes of the vowel (akṣara); another is established in the consonant (vitta); another is of the same class (samānajāti); and another bestows the sibilants (ūṣman). 67–68.
Just as the breath of a young snake is gentle, so too should the *ūṣman* be applied, devoid of the letter *ha*. The wise declare that the *ūṣman* is the expansion of the suffixes. 69.
They indeed prohibit that very [sandhi], as illustrated by the example *ā ī ū e*.
(70) I shall now declare the eight vowels and their specific characteristics:
the *jātya*, the *abhinihita*, the *kṣaipra*, and likewise another, the *praśliṣṭa*. (71)
The *pādavṛtta* (foot-division) should be understood in this manner. Regarding vowels:

when occurring within a single word (*ekapada*), a circumflex (*svarita*) preceded by a grave (*nīca*) vowel is called *jātya*. He says "within a single word" [to exclude cases like *sadyas*]. When preceded by a grave vowel, a circumflex vowel that is followed by the letters *ya* or *va* is *jātya*. For example: *jātyaṃ manuṣyān*, *sudyeti*, *camvīva dhānyam*, *kanyā iva svaḥ*, *vīryam*. Thus he has said; and whatever other words have such characteristics are included. When an *a*-vowel is elided between these two acute (*udātta*) vowels, and there is a *riphita* [consonant], they know that as *abhinihita*. Where the *a*-vowel is dropped, that is known as *abhinihita*. 73.

As in: *kukkuṭaḥ* — *asi kukkuṭo'si*; *vedaḥ* — *asi vedo'si*; *bhāgaḥ* — *asi bhāgo'si*; *mārutaḥ* — *asi māruto'si*; *śvātraḥ* — *asi śvātro'si*; *te* — *apsarasām te'psarasām*; *te* — *avantu te'vantu*; *kaḥ* — *asi ko'si*; *saḥ* — *ahaṃ so'ham*. Thus, whatever other words there may be with such characteristics: when the vowels *i* and *u* become udātta, or when *y* and *v* occur in certain cases within a word that is otherwise always anudātta, one should recognize this as the characteristic of the *kṣaipra* sandhi. (74)

As in *tryambakam* [and] *tryambakam*, *drvannaḥ* [and] *drvannaḥ*, *vīḍvaṅgaḥ* [and] *vīḍvaṅgaḥ*, *vājyarvan* [and] *vājyarvan*; so too it has been said regarding other words that possess such characteristics: wherever an *i*-vowel is seen joined with an *i*-vowel, and where an acute accent (*udātta*) is fused with a grave accent (*anudātta*), [it is a case of *praśleṣa*]. 75. As in *abhīndhatām* [and] *abhīndhatām*, *abhīmam* [and] *abhīmam*, *vīhi* [and] *vīhi*.

"Like *srucī-iva*, like *srucī-iva*; like *camvī-iva*, like *camvī-iva*. Thus he says; for whatever other words there may be of this same character—whatever word in the Veda has a circumflex (*svarita*) preceded by an acute (*udātta*)—all such cases are called the *bahusvāra tairovyañjana*. 76.
*Iḍe*, *rante*, *havye*, *kāmye*, *candre*, *jyote*, *adite*, *sarasvati*, *mahi*, and *viśruti*—these are [the names].

Thus it is said: "Furthermore, whatever other words there may be that possess such characteristics, if there is a circumflex (*svarita*) immediately following a pause (*avagraha*)," [they are to be treated as such].
One should recognize that as *tairo-virāma* if there is an avagraha (separation) following an acute accent (*udātta*).

For example: *gomad iti gomat*, *gopatāv iti gopatau*, *prapreti prapra*, *vitateti vitatā*, *samiddha iti samiddhaḥ*. Likewise, it is said: "And whatever other words have such characteristics," [as well as] where a hiatus (*vivṛti*) is observed between an acute (*svara*) and a circumflex (*svarita*), there the *svāra* occurs at the pause of the foot (*pādavṛtta*). Examples are: *śvitra ādityeti śvitra ādityānām* (i.e., *śvitraḥ-ādityānām*, *śvitra ādityānām*), *putra īdhe putra īdhe* (i.e., *putraḥ-īdhe*, *putra īdhe*), and *dātra edhi dātre edhi*.

*kaḥ-īm*, *kaīm*; *tāḥ-asya*, *tāasya*. For thus it has been said: "Whatever other words exist with such characteristics—where there is a low-pitched vowel (*nīca*) between two acute-pitched vowels (*udātta*), that is the pause (*avagraha*). It should be so treated; 'tanūnaptrā' is an illustration of this [case of] trembling. (78) As in *tanūnaptrā* for *tanūnaptre*; *tanūnapād* for *tanūnapāt*; *tanūnapātam*.
To Tanūnapāt. For thus he has said: "Those words which are indicative marks.
Thus ends the recitation of the words of Yājñavalkya’s statements in the Vaiśeṣika collection of eight words.
That which is recorded as being contrary to the Mādhyamdina recension should be understood accordingly;
however, no accentuation here is observed, as the udātta and anudātta are distinct [only in that context].
2.1 The vowels, the stops (sparśa), the semi-vowels (antaḥstha), and the sibilants (ūṣman) [are the phonemes].

The gutturals, the root-linguals, the palatals, the retroflexes, the dentals, the labials, the semivowels (*yama*), the *visarjanīya*, and the particles (*nipāta*) have the vowels as their deities; they are white and possess various deities. The stops (*sparśa*) are black. The semi-vowels (*antasthā*) are tawny (*kapila*). The sibilants (*ūṣman*) are ruddy (*aruṇa*). The *yamas* are blue. The nasalized sounds (*nāsikya*) are green. The *anusvāra* is yellow. The *jihvāmūlīya* is red. The *upadhmānīya* is yellow. The *visarjanīya* is white. The *raṅga* is variegated. The nasalized vowel (*anunāsikya*) is blue.

One should know that the nasal (*nāsikya*) belongs to the internal and middle [positions]. It is traditionally taught that there are two types called "acute" (*udātta*). Regarding the occurrence of *ud*, *an-ud*, and *ni-pāta*, as well as the first prefix (*upasarga*), and both nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*)—including prefixes and particles (*nipāta*)—one might ask: what are their deities? Furthermore, among the syllables (*akṣara*), which are the males, which are the females, and which are the neuters? To this we reply: the gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*), beginning with *a*, belong to Agni; the retroflexes (*jihvāmūlīya*), beginning with *k*, belong to Nirṛti; the palatals (*tālavya*), beginning with *c*, belong to Soma; the cerebrals (*mūrdhanya*), beginning with *ṭ*, belong to Vāyu; and the dentals (*dantya*), beginning with *t*, belong to Rudra.

The labials belong to Āśvinī; the letters beginning with *pa* belong to Vaiśvadevī; and the remaining letters, such as *aṃ* and so forth, belong to Brāhmaṇī. Furthermore, the vowels are to be known as belonging to Brāhmaṇī; likewise, the first, second, third, and fourth letters of each group (*varga*) belong to the Earth-rulers (Kṣatriyas).

The fifth letters of the classes, as well as the semivowels and the sibilants, together with the letter *ha*, are proclaimed to be the Śūdras. Names of white color are declared [to be Brahmins], while those considered red are [Kṣatriyas].
The *upasargas* are the Kapiñjalas, and the *nipātakas* are the Kṛṣṇas.
Those of the Bhārgava lineage are declared to be the Bhāradvājas;
the *upasargas* are the Vāsiṣṭhas, while the *nipātas* are remembered as the Kāśyapas.
A yellow-colored *upasarga* is a *nipāta*, while a black-colored one is declared to be entirely *saumya*. A *vāyavya* name is seen as such;
however, an *upasarga* is *āgneya*, and a *nipāta* is remembered as *vāruṇa*.
The first [consonants] as well as the semivowels (*antastha*) are proclaimed to be feminine;
those who discern gender say that the remaining letters are neuter.

Indra is the deity of nouns, Varuṇa of prefixes, and Āditya of the entire collection of vowels. The *visarjanīya*, the *yamas*, and the [unaspirated] stops are masculine. The letters *ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m* and *y, r, l, v* are feminine.

The remaining syllables are neuter gender. Sandhi is of four kinds: elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), modification of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*), and preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). For example: therein, elision occurs—as in *ayakṣmāḥ mā* becoming *ayakṣmāmā*; *śatatejāḥ vāyuḥ* becoming *śatatejāvāyuḥ*; and *tigmatejāḥ dviṣataḥ* becoming *tigmatejādviṣataḥ*. Thus ends elision.

There is *āgama* (augmentation): as in *pratyak somaḥ*, *pratyaṅ somaḥ*, *prāksomaḥ*, *prāṅsomaḥ*, *asmān sīte*, *asmāntsīte*, *trīn samudrān*, *trīntsamudrān*. Such is *āgama*. There is *vikāra* (modification): *ā-idam* becomes *edam*; *ā-ime* becomes *eme*; *ā-iṣṭayaḥ* becomes *eṣṭayaḥ*; *pra-iṣitaḥ* becomes *preṣitaḥ*. Such is *vikāra*. There is *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention): as in *āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*, *yuñjānaḥ prathamam*, *aditiḥ ṣoḍaśākṣareṇa*, *devo vaḥ savitā*. Such is *prakṛtibhāva*.
Like lightning in the sky, like a gem on a thread, this is the cutting of the *vivṛti*s; it is like a pair of scissors among the ignorant.
Where no *saṃdhi* is seen between two vowels, [that is the cutting].
In that regard, the "unfoldment" (vivṛtti) is to be understood; "He who [is] the Lord" is the illustration.
There are four types of unfoldment: the ant-like, the ripening, the following the calf, and the accompanying the calf. 8–9.
The five colors proceed from the Vajrin who destroys and annihilates;
*aha*, *ra*, *pra*, *ha*, and *ra* are to be known as the examples for *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *o*.
The ant is long at both ends; "it was from the navel"—this is the illustration.
The example for both [types] when short is "pākavatī" and "vina indra";
the example at the end for one releasing the calves is "tā na āvoḍham aśvinā.
The example for one following the calves at the beginning when long is "tā asya. 11–12.

Kariṇī, Kurviṇī, Hariṇī, Hāriṇī, and likewise Haṃsapadā—these are the five *svarabhaktis*. (13) Kariṇī occurs in the conjunction of *ra* and *ha*; Kurviṇī occurs in the conjunction of *la*, *ha*, and *ka*.
One should know that *hariṇī* occurs in the combination of *ra* and *ṣa*, while *hārita* occurs in the combination of *ṛ* and *ṣa*.
That which is named *haṃsapadā* consists of *repha* (the letter *r*) and *ṣa*; one should know *hariṇī* in the combination of *ha* and *ra*, and *kurviṇī* in the combination of *ha* and *la*.
"Devam barhiḥ" is for the *kariṇī*; "upavalha" is for the *kurviṇī*;
"hariṇī arepasaḥ" and "śatavalśā" are said to be for the *hāriṇī*;
and likewise "varṣovarṣīyasī" and "haṃsapadā."
One employing *svarabhakti* should avoid three defects:
the vowel *i*, the vowel *u*, and likewise the defect of being swallowed (*grasta*).
This definition was proclaimed by the wise Yājñavalkya. (17–18)
For the sake of the perfection of correct recitation and out of a desire for the welfare of his disciples,
pronouncing the vowel of the half-mora slightly separately as if it were diminished—
at the *ṛ*-sound, at the *h*-sound, and at the heart, throat, and mind— (19).
This [svarita] is not prescribed in any way when it precedes a prior member, nor in any way when it follows a subsequent member; neither in its accent nor in its duration is a svarita ever ordained.
However, that which precedes a subsequent member, and that which follows a prior member—[in those cases, it is so ordained].

When there is a conjunction of both halves of the two [halves], the wise one should apply the *svāra* accent. However, in a conjunction, the subsequent [vowel] has the meaning of *svāra*, while the subsequent [consonant] is named after the conjunction;
for a consonant that is conjoined, the preceding syllable does not have the *svāra* accent.
One should begin the left eyebrow with an *udātta* [vowel] and an *anudātta*;
from the *udātta*, one should place the *svarita* and *udātta* in succession on the right.
Those [vowels] which follow a *svarita* as *anudātta*s are called *pracaya*.
Those who contemplate the true meaning say that even when [the vowels] are uttered with a single tone (ekasvara),
one should suppress the tone where an accumulation is perceived;
where there is only a circumflex (svarita) and it is soft, there the wise man should let it fall.
Just as a powerful king seizes the kingdom of one who is weak, so too does the letter *a*, having encountered a consonant (*vyañjana*), seize the vowel (*svara*).
There is nothing higher than the high, and likewise, nothing lower than the low.
27. Due to the similarity of syllables and their connection, [the vowels] are also situated in the low [register] when following a low [consonant].
28. A vowel is high (*udātta*), a vowel is low (*anudātta*), and a vowel is circumflex (*svarita*).
Because they are dominated by these vowels, the consonant is likewise possessed of tone (*sasvara*).
The consonants follow wherever that vowel resides;

for the teachers declare that the threefold accentuation (traisvarya) has the vowel as its primary element. One should know the consonant to be like a gem and the vowel to be like the string [upon which it is strung].
Teachers desire evenness, while scholars desire the division of words (paḍaccheda).
Women desire sweetness, while other people desire what is drawn out (vikṛṣṭa).
They do not follow the udātta accent, nor likewise the nīca or the svarita.
One should recognize that as having a circumflex accent (visvara), devoid of long and short [vowels].
Among the syllables *hari*, *varuṇa*, *vareṇya*, and the *dhārā-puruṣas*, the *repha* is circumflex; the *nakāra* has the form of the remainder (*śeṣākāra*), and these *nakāras* are circumflex. 32.
The two *varuṇa* syllables are *svarita*;
"uduttamaṃ," "varuṇa," "dhārayaṃvāro," "rudhārā," and "urudhārā"—
these are either one-mora or two-mora *svarita* when they occur here as a syllable.
Of that [syllable], the first half-measure indeed belongs to the former, and the remainder occurs thereafter.
When the word ending in *na* is preceded by a word ending in *śmaśrubhiḥ*, one should not employ the letter *cha*; rather, one should pronounce the *ña-śa* sandhi. 33–34.
The syllable *oṃ* is to be known as the *pluta*; the second is the *pluta* submerged [in the heart];
the third is *lājīṃ chācīṃ*; and "he entered" (*viveśa*) is the fourth.
"Was it below? is the fifth, and "was it above? is the sixth. (35)

The seventh [syllable] is indeed remembered as being between the eyebrows, while the eighth does not exist at all. When the hand is positioned in a raised place, the *svarita* accent is not applicable; however, when it moves to a lowered position, then the *svarita* occurs.

The letters ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa are constantly seen in their places of junction when joined with their own respective groups; one should not effect a release (sandhi) there. However, when a word ending in *ta* is followed by the letter *sa*, [one should proceed accordingly].

One should not perform reduplication (pratyārambha) when the word *pāpa* follows; this is the illustration. When a word ending in the letter *ka* precedes and the letter *sa* follows, one should recognize it as having the same sound as *kha*; "bhikṣakṣa" is the illustration.

When a word ending in the letter *t* is preceded by a word ending in a *ca*-group consonant (*c*, *ch*, *j*, *jh*, *ñ*), one should effect elision (*mokṣa*) there; this is the illustration regarding what is sinful. When a word ending in the letter *ṅ* is preceded by a word ending in the letter *s*, [the same applies].

One should understand [the doubling] as a *ka*-savarna when the word *prāk soma* follows; for example, *saṃskr̥ta*. One should understand [the doubling] as a *ṭa*-savarna when a word ending in *ṭa* precedes and the letter *sa* follows; for example, *saṃmr̥ḍ* and *saṃbhṛta*.
One should know that when a word ending in *takāra* (t) precedes and the letter *sakāra* (s) follows, it becomes the *ch-savarṇa* (the sound *cch*). "Tatsavituḥ" is the illustration.
[Likewise,] when a word ending in *nakāra* (n) precedes and the letter *sakāra* (s) follows...
One should recognize it as having the same vowel-color (savarna) when there are three oceans; this is the illustration.
When the word *anuṣṭup* precedes and the letter *śa* follows, one should recognize it as having the same vowel-color (*chāsavarṇa*); "anuṣṭucchāradī" is the illustration.

When the word ending in *m* is followed by a homogeneous vowel, one should know that the *m* becomes homogeneous with that vowel; this is illustrated by the example "imaṃ me. However, when a single-mora (*mātrika*) vowel precedes, the *anusvāra* is two morae (*dvimātraka*).

A *mātrika* [vowel] following a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) should be known as having two *mātrās*. An *anusvāra* preceded by an *ṛ*-vowel or a consonant shall have two *mātrās*, whether it follows a short or a long vowel— as in the case of "devānām̐ hṛdayebhyaḥ."
Where a closed (saṃvṛta) vowel is seen above an anusvāra, one should know that it is long; "the tip of the ear" (śrotāgra) is the illustration.
Where a consonant cluster (saṃyoga) is seen above an anusvāra, [it is likewise long].

One should know that to be short; "sam̐sthā" is the illustrative example. Furthermore, when an *anusvāra* follows a long vowel or a consonant, it should be understood as short according to the optionality [prescribed] specifically for mantras.

Luminosity (obhāva), expansion (vivṛtti), the sibilants ś, ṣ, and s, the letter r, the root of the tongue (jihvāmūla), and the labio-dental (upadhmāna)— these are the eightfold movement of the *uṣman* sounds;
just as there is a connection with their inherent nature when followed by vowels such as *u* and others.
One should know that which ends in a vowel to be of such a kind; any other [consonant] distinct from a sibilant (*ūṣman*) is also [of that kind].
A sibilant arising from both [vowels] is designated as *keli*.
That sibilant directed toward the open [vowels] is to be known as *vikaṭānanā*.
*Līḍhā* and *atilīḍhā* are proclaimed to occur with the letters *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*;
they are to be known as *viṭhakā* and *śaṭhā* when occurring with the *jihvāmūlīya* and the letter *ra*.
Together with the *upadhmānīya*, one should designate that [sequence] as *puṣpiṇī*.
One should designate as "easily attainable" (*sulabhā*) that which possesses heat (*ūṣman*) elsewhere;
one should know it to be slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) at the beginning and end of a word, as well as during the pause (*avagraha*), and one should perform [the recitation] at that time.

That which occurs at the beginning of a word, at the beginning of a foot (pāda), and in the case of the elision (*avagraha*) of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), should be known as *ya*; that which is otherwise is remembered as *ya*.
Furthermore, that which follows a prefix (*upasarga*) is also seen to be [treated as] the beginning of a word.

They are slightly articulated (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) such that they follow the *vidyutpada* meter; if the particles *vā*, *vām*, or *vāi* express the meaning of "you" (*tvad*), or if they are used optionally at the beginning of a word to signify "or" (*vā*), they are traditionally known as slightly articulated.
In the *Vibhāṣā*, there would be the vowel *e* [as a substitute], and likewise, when followed by these words, it occurs after a word-final position;
the same applies to *bhavanti*. Furthermore, whatever grammatical rule applies to that [word-final] position would also apply to the letter *v*.
Wherever there may be a distinction, that is now being stated:
the letter *va* is said to be of three kinds—long (*guru*), short (*laghu*), and short-final (*laghūttara*). It is long at the beginning, short in the middle, and short-final at the end of a word.
He who studies it in a whisper and with haste is known as "Hṛdi-saṃjñaka";
he prevails even over thousands of forms and embodied beings.
Yet, those men who are dull-witted and stubborn do not grasp this fivefold knowledge.
Free from laziness and disease, and with a mind that has forgotten [worldly distractions], he acquires knowledge— fearing praise as a snake fears its own coils, fearing honor as if it were hell,
and fearing women as if they were ogresses.
One should not delay over food, nor should one be bound by attachment to women;
for the sake of knowledge, a seeker should travel even to the furthest distance like a garuḍa or a swan,
just as a man digging with a spade eventually reaches water.
Likewise, one who desires pleasure attains knowledge from the teacher;
if one seeking pleasure abandons knowledge, or one seeking knowledge abandons pleasure,
how can there be knowledge for those who seek pleasure, and how can there be pleasure for those who seek knowledge?
Knowledge multiplied a hundred times and further recited a thousand times will come to the tip of one's tongue, just as water flows to a low-lying place;
knowledge multiplied by a hundred remains stable when multiplied by a thousand.
With a thousand times a hundred [repetitions], he stands facing the opposite direction;
through the practice of yoga, he effects the dissolution of stone; for one who has become soft like a water-jar, what is not accomplished through practice?
Knowledge is acquired through service to the teacher, or by means of abundant wealth, or else through knowledge itself; a fourth means is not found.
For knowledge devoid of service is accompanied by the qualities of a dull intellect.
And for that barren woman in her youth, knowledge shall not bear fruit;
for those who seek knowledge, sleep does not remain long in their eyes, unlike noble horses that sleep for only half a measure at a time.
Just as an anthill is built up by ants with particles of dust,
yet there is no power or strength therein— exertion is the cause;
so too, having observed the depletion of collyrium and the accumulation of the anthill.
One should make each day fruitful through acts of giving, study, and ritual work; one should set aside a third part for food and condiments,
and a fourth part for the movement of air.

One should know that the letter *ha* joined with the fifth [consonants] and also conjoined with the semivowels (*antastha*) is guttural; they say it is palatal when uncombined. Wherever the letter *ha* stands first and a semivowel or similar sound follows as the subsequent [element], [it is guttural].
If it should be separated at the time of word-division but joined in the *saṃhitā*, that is the "aurasa" [breath-sound];
it is known as having the resonance of a cloud or a drum, arising from the heart of water;
thus the sound should be employed like the roar of a lion.
Just as clouds make such a sound in the month of Bhādrapada, so too, having reached the mountain cave, they saw Śukra milking [the cows]; meanwhile,
the remaining monkeys leaped up and fell down in battle.
Thus should the phonemes (varṇas) be articulated; here and there is an illustration of them:
just as a mother with a son kisses her own biological child out of affection, so should the phonemes be articulated—this is the illustration for one who is practicing.

In the section on victory, [the syllables] *dur*, *da*, *ra*, *ja*, *ya*, *de*, *śa*, *ca*, *pra*, *pha*, *te*, *ṣu*, *na*, *yā*, *pya*, and *yā* should be employed; "the foam of the waters" (*apām phena*) is the illustrative example,
just as men burdened by heavy loads heave sighs upon the earth.
The phonemes should be articulated in this manner: even in the phrase "saṃbhṛta ity api," one should utter two *ka*-sounds as in "kukkuṭaḥ" and "kāmalubdhaḥ.
The phonemes should be articulated thus; such is the view regarding the word "kukkuṭo 'si."

Just as a mare, upon seeing a horse, undergoes a transformation of her womb, so too should the phonemes (varṇas) be employed; this is the view that [the recitation] should be accompanied by the sound of a drum. Furthermore, when the stage has been entered, one should not swallow the preceding syllable.
One should employ a long vowel and subsequently perform the nasalization (*nāsikya*);
just as a woman from Saurāṣṭra pronounces "arām," so should the letter *raṅga* be uttered, excluding the letter *ṅ*.

A consonant with two morae (*dvimātrika*) or one with one mora (*mātrika*), when resting upon the root of the nose, is pronounced at the end together with the fifth [consonants] as nasalized (*sānunāsika*).
For example, a woman from Saurāṣṭra speaks thus: *ārām̐*.
In this way, one should understand the color [of the letter] excluding the sound *ṅ*;
immediately following the letter *m*, that which is the color there is colored by all nasal sounds (*anunāsika*); this is the intermediate *upadhānikā*.

The *upadhānika* vowels are produced from the palate (*tālu*), while those ending in *ra* and *va* are produced from the throat (*kaṇṭha*). That which is nasalized by all [the following consonants] is produced from the nose; its resonance is like that of bronze.
It should be soft and consist of two morae; it should be "possessing rain" (vṛṣṭimat), as illustrated by this:
just as a tigress carries her cubs with her teeth, yet does not wound them—being afraid of their falling or being crushed—so should one employ the phonemes.
Neither too sweet nor indistinct, yet distinct and not strained—
such were the notes of the protector’s single region, which did not reach Śaṅkara,
just as a well-intoxicated lord of elephants places one foot after another with measured care.
In this way, each word, including its beginning and end, should be shown separately.

These six are the lowest of reciters: one who sings, one who is too fast, one who shakes his head, one who reads exactly as written, one who does not understand the meaning, and one with a weak voice.
Sweetness, clarity of syllables, clear enunciation of words, melodious tone, composure, and equality of tempo— these six are the qualities of a reciter;
and a group of four syllables should be repeated again and again.
That which repeats a word twice or thrice is indeed an *āvarta*;
for example, "dhāmne dhāmne" and "yajurṣe yajuṣe" are illustrations. Furthermore, O slender-waisted one, there is also that wherein a word is either omitted or augmented.
That should be understood as figurative usage (upacāra); "both are Suścandrā" is the illustration.
Now, there are seven kinds of composite masses:
the iron mass, the wooden mass, the wool mass, the flame mass, the clay mass, the wind mass, and the diamond mass.
One should know that the *yamādi* [consonants] are like the iron mass, while those ending with the semivowels (*sāntastha*) are like the wooden mass.
One should designate the semi-vowels (antastha), excluding *ya* and *ma*, as the "ūrṇā-piṇḍa" (the woolly ball). When there is a conjunction with *ya* and *ma*, no distinction is perceived;
one should know that *ya* and *ma* are bodiless, while the semi-vowels are the leaders of the piṇḍas.
The clusters of flames with the *nāsikya* and *anusvāra* are made of clay;
those with the *upadhmānīya* are clusters of wind at the root of the tongue for the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*),
just like what is called a cluster of iron.
I do not stretch out cooked offerings like fire; for just as a wooden block is called "horse," so the sun is said to be "the conqueror of all."
In that regard, what is called a "ball of wool" is as follows:
it is when one thinks, "in this," "in that," or "in yonder";
and therein, what is called a "ball of flame" is as follows:
"Brahmā, Agni, I take"—thus it is there; that which is called the "clod of earth" is like the preparers who prepare. Therein, that which is called the "clod of air" is as follows:
O God Savitṛ, yoking first at the beginning of the day, he becomes one who is "asleep on the summit."
In that regard, what is called the "vajra-piṇḍa" is as follows:
it occurs when *iṣkṛti* and *niṣkṛti* become *ṛksāma*, being joined from the very beginning with the letter *ṣa* and the letter *sa*.
Having attained this vowel, the Agniṣvātta-s are the illustration; with the first letter *ṭha*, joined with the letter *tha*,
having attained this vowel, the Adhiṣṭhāna-s are the illustration.
First of all, joined with the letter *ṇa* and indeed with the letter *na*,
having attained this vowel— of which "the twenty-ninth" and "the thirty-third" are the illustrations—
it is first of all joined with the letter *ra* and indeed with the letter *na*.
Having reached this "dyed" [syllable], there is the illustration "one who has rained.
These letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are explained as being black in color, presided over by Saturn (*śanaiścara*).
The four semivowels—*ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*—are tawny in color and presided over by Fire (*agni*).
The four sibilants—śa, ṣa, sa, and ha—are of the color of dawn and have the Sun as their deity.

There are thirty-three consonants (*vyañjana*), which are of four kinds according to their mode of articulation (*karaṇa*): the contact sounds (*spṛṣṭa*), the semi-vowels (*antasthā*), the sibilants (*ūṣman*), and the aspirates (*nivṛta*). These are further characterized as being either unaspirated (*aspṛṣṭa*) or closed (*saṃvṛta*).

The voiced consonants (*ghoṣa*) are twenty; they are *ga, ja, ḍa, da, ba*; *gha, jha, ḍha, dha, bha*; *ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma*; and *ya, ra, la, va*—these thirteen are the unvoiced (*aghoṣa*). They are *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa*; *kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha*; and *śa, ṣa, sa*.
There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes:
chest, throat, head, palate, teeth, root of the tongue, lips, and nose; among these, the two *ha*s (the first and second) are produced from the chest.

A, ā, and ā³—these three are gutturals; ṣ, ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, ḍh, ṇ, and ṣ—these six are cerebrals; i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au, and aṃ—aṃ—aḥ—these ten are palatals; c, ch, j, jh, ñ, y, ś, and ṣ—these eight are palatals; t, th, d, dh, n, s, t, th, d, dh, n, and s—these ten are cerebrals; t, th, d, dh, n, and s—these six are dentals; p, ph, b, bh, m, and h—these six are labials. Thus [the consonants are enumerated]. i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au, and aṃ—aṃ—aḥ—these eighteen are vowels. c, ch, j, jh, ñ, y, ś, and ṣ—these eight are palatals. t, th, d, dh, n, and s—these six are cerebrals. t, th, d, dh, n, and s—these six are dentals. p, ph, b, bh, m, and h—these six are labials. The eight dentals are *ta, tha, da, dha, na, la, ṣa*, and *la*; the eleven labials are *pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ma, mā, ū, ū, ū, ū³*; the *ch* and *upadhmānīya* are among those [consonants];
and the single retroflex (*repha*) is the dental-rooted (*dantamūlīya*).
The five jihvāmūlīya consonants are *kuṃ*, *khuṃ*, *guṃ*, *ghuṃ*, and *ṅuṃ*;
the four *yama*s are *km*, *khm*, *gm*, and *ghm*; the first *rakta* is to be known as *kuṃ*, *khuṃ*, *guṃ*, *ghuṃ*, and *ṅuṃ*; and the other is *sak*.
They say the third is the "seat" (sadman), and the fourth is "the one to be blown upon" (upadhmāna). The first two are the labial and the nasal; they rest upon the lips and the nose.
The second [of these] is both guttural and dental, resting at the root of the nose.
One should indicate the third [Yama] at the root of the tongue and the palate;
the fourth is nasalized and is said to be in the heart and the throat.
The fifth syllable is joined with the first quarter of the fifth [vowel].
Because in that [state] all turn back, like kinsmen from a cremation ground; whatever consists of speech in the world, all of it is established here— all of it is established here— thus,
when the letter *ṛ* is followed by a long vowel (*tī*), there is a double-mora anusvāra.
When combined with subsequent sounds, it is called "short" by the wise.
Thus ends the Śrī Yājñavalkyaśikṣā.
